resources.string: A connectivity interruption that affects your own household.
Correlated wireless disruption across several households and elevated neighborhood alerts.
Shown briefly on older Android versions while a connectivity report is uploaded.
Grey: monitoring inactive or status unknown. This does not mean everything is fine.
Neighborhood Watchdog notices when home Wi-Fi drops in several nearby homes at about the same time, and tells the neighborhood. It detects unusual patterns. It cannot tell you what caused them.

Only this phone\'s own network connection: whether it is on Wi-Fi, whether the internet is reachable, whether mobile data is available, and the Wi-Fi signal strength and band when Android provides them.

Short connectivity events (for example \"Wi-Fi lost\" with the time), a random install ID, the app version and the Android version. There is no account: no email address, no password and no sign-in. You can read every event the app sends on the Transparency screen.

No location or GPS. No Wi-Fi name, Wi-Fi password or router password. No browsing history, websites, messages, contacts, camera or microphone. No hardware identifiers. The app never accesses security cameras or other accounts.

When Wi-Fi fails, the report cannot travel over Wi-Fi. The app asks Android for the mobile data connection and sends the small report over it. If mobile data is not available either, the report is kept on the phone and sent later with its original time.

Android limits what apps may do in the background to save battery. The app does not keep a permanent service running. It listens while Android keeps it in memory and checks in about every 15 minutes. Times when it could not monitor are reported as gaps, never hidden.

The server compares events from households that are near each other. One home losing Wi-Fi is usually a router, power or provider problem. Several homes with different providers losing Wi-Fi within a short time is unusual and raises an alert. An alert describes a pattern; it is not proof of a cause.
Settings has a monitoring switch. When it is off, the app tells the server once that you paused monitoring and then stops observing and reporting.

Settings has \"Leave neighborhood\". It deletes this phone and everything it reported from the service, stops monitoring, and removes the queued events, the home-network fingerprint and the install ID from this phone.
Paste the whole link or only the code at its end.
Joining needs the invitation link your neighborhood organizer sent to your home. Open that link on this phone, or paste it here. There is no account and nothing to sign in to.

The app reports this phone\'s own connectivity events (for example \"Wi-Fi lost\" with the time) under a random install ID. The street, and the house number if you give one, are used to group the phones of one home and are never shown to other residents. No name, email address, location, Wi-Fi name or browsing data is collected. Leaving deletes this phone and everything it reported.
By tapping Join you confirm that you have read the privacy summary and that this phone may report its connectivity events.
Enter the name of your street.
This phone is no longer part of the neighborhood network: it left or was removed. To join again, ask your neighborhood organizer for a new invitation link.
That does not look like an invitation link.
This phone has joined. Two short steps are left.

Notifications are how the app tells you about a household connectivity interruption or an elevated neighborhood alert. Without them you only see alerts when you open the app. Monitoring works either way.

A phone also loses Wi-Fi when you leave the house. To tell the difference, the app can remember your home network. If this phone is connected to your home Wi-Fi right now, confirm it below.
The app stores a scrambled fingerprint of the router address on this phone only. It is never sent anywhere. The Wi-Fi name is not read and location permission is not used.

The score adds up the indicators below. A higher score means the pattern is more unusual, not that a cause is proven.

The app reports connectivity events only. It does not use location, and it does not read the Wi-Fi name, browsing activity or anything else on this phone. The Transparency screen shows exactly what is sent.

Leaving deletes this phone and everything it reported from the service. Monitoring stops, and the queued events, the home-network fingerprint and the install ID are removed from this phone. There is no account, so nothing else is left to delete.
This phone and everything it reported are deleted from the service, and the app\'s data is removed from this phone. This cannot be undone. To join again you need a new invitation link.

What Android does not allow or the app cannot know
In the background Android may pause or stop the app. The app then misses changes until its next check, about every 15 minutes, and reports the gap.
Battery saver, Doze and background restrictions can delay checks and uploads further.
A phone is on one Wi-Fi band at a time. The app cannot check whether other bands were affected and never says they were.
The app sees connectivity only. It cannot measure radio interference and cannot identify the cause of a disruption.
Sending a report over mobile data is attempted when Wi-Fi fails, but is not guaranteed. Reports that cannot be sent are kept and sent later with their original time.
No independent security review has been published for this build.
The secret this phone received when it joined and the home-network fingerprint are encrypted with a key held in the Android Keystore. App data is excluded from device backups.
Events are stored on this phone first and removed only after the server answered. Tap an event to see exactly what is sent.
